Atmospheric Rivers — Water in Motion

A source-verified museum-quality direct-canvas infographic showing how a long, narrow corridor of wind-driven atmospheric water vapor crosses an ocean, rises over coastal mountains, and produces rain or snow, with both water-supply benefits and flood or slope hazards.

Research behind the infographic

  • Atmospheric rivers are relatively long, narrow regions of enhanced water-vapor transport in the atmosphere. [1] [2]
  • Atmospheric rivers transport much of the water vapor moving outside the tropics and can carry moisture from lower latitudes toward higher latitudes. [1] [2]
  • Water vapor within an atmospheric river is transported by winds, so both moisture content and wind contribute to vapor transport. [1] [2]
  • Atmospheric-river water vapor is concentrated primarily in the lower atmosphere rather than forming a liquid river in the sky. [2]
  • When moist air reaches land and is forced upward over mountains, cooling and condensation can release the transported water as rain or snow. [1] [2]
  • Atmospheric rivers vary greatly in size, strength, shape, and impacts. [1] [2]
  • Weaker atmospheric rivers can provide beneficial rain and snowpack that support water supplies. [1] [2]
  • Strong or slow-moving atmospheric rivers can produce extreme precipitation, flooding, landslides, and debris-flow hazards. [1] [2]
  • Satellite, radar, aircraft, and weather-model observations are used to study and forecast atmospheric rivers. [1]
  • Integrated vapor transport is a useful way to represent the combined movement of atmospheric water vapor by the wind. [1] [2]
  • Atmospheric rivers are not all hazardous; their effects depend on intensity, duration, landfall location, terrain, and watershed vulnerability. [1] [2]

Sources

  1. What are atmospheric rivers? — National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration
  2. Rivers in the Sky: 6 Facts You Should Know about Atmospheric Rivers — U.S. Geological Survey

Fire Cloud Chimney — How a Pyrocumulonimbus Lofts Smoke

A source-verified museum-quality direct infographic explaining how intense wildfire heat and smoke can build from pyrocumulus into a deep pyrocumulonimbus and, in some events, inject smoke into the upper troposphere or lower stratosphere.

Research behind the infographic

  • A pyrocumulonimbus, or pyroCb, is a thunderstorm-like cloud produced when an intense fire lofts enough heat, smoke, and moisture to drive deep convection. [1] [2]
  • PyroCb development can grow from precursor pyrocumulus convection above a wildfire, but not every pyrocumulus becomes a large pyrocumulonimbus. [2]
  • A strong pyroCb acts as a vertical chimney that carries smoke through the troposphere and can inject it into the upper troposphere and lower stratosphere. [1] [2]
  • Smoke that reaches the stratosphere can spread over very large distances and remain aloft longer than smoke confined to the lower troposphere. [1]
  • PyroCb smoke injection is studied with aircraft remote sensing, in-situ instruments, ground-based sensors, satellites, and atmospheric models. [1] [2]
  • Researchers are investigating which fires produce pyroCbs, what controls direct stratospheric injection and plume magnitude, and how injected smoke changes upper-atmospheric composition and radiation. [2]
  • PyroCb occurrence and injection height depend on the coupled fire and atmospheric environment, so a large wildfire does not automatically produce a stratospheric smoke plume. [1] [2]
  • The visible cloud may show a dark smoke-fed lower column and a brighter ice-cloud tower or anvil above it. [1]

Sources

  1. Flying through a Fire Cloud — NASA Earth Observatory
  2. INjected Smoke and PYRocumulonimbus Experiment (INSPYRE) — National Center for Atmospheric Research Earth Observing Laboratory

Gecko Grip — Dry Adhesion Without Glue

A museum-quality direct-canvas guide to how Tokay gecko toe pads use branching setae, spatula contact, van der Waals attraction, directional loading, and peeling release to create reversible dry adhesion.

Research behind the infographic

  • Tokay gecko toe pads carry microscopic hairs called setae, and each seta branches into much smaller terminal pads called spatulae. [1] [2]
  • The hierarchical branching from toe pad to setae to spatulae creates extensive close contact with a surface. [1] [2]
  • Experiments support van der Waals forces as the primary mechanism of dry adhesion in Tokay gecko setae. [1]
  • Gecko dry adhesion does not require secreted glue or suction. [1] [2]
  • Tokay gecko setae adhered similarly to strongly hydrophobic and strongly hydrophilic surfaces when both surfaces were polarizable, arguing against capillary adhesion as necessary. [1]
  • Simply touching a seta to a surface is insufficient for strong attachment; loading it toward the surface and slightly along the surface engages adhesion. [2]
  • The directional geometry of setae and spatulae makes attachment dependent on loading direction. [1] [2]
  • Geckos detach rapidly by changing angle and peeling their toes away, which progressively reduces contact rather than breaking every contact at once. [2]
  • The adhesive system works without leaving a glue residue on the contacted surface. [2]
  • Setal-tip size and shape, rather than high surface polarity, are central to the measured adhesion mechanism. [1]
  • Subdividing an adhesive surface into many small contacts increases contact density and is a design principle for gecko-inspired dry adhesives. [1]
  • Natural surfaces can be more challenging than clean laboratory glass; waxy leaf coatings may hinder close intermolecular contact. [2]
  • The Tokay gecko, Gekko gecko, is native to Southeast Asia. [2]

Sources

  1. Evidence for van der Waals adhesion in gecko setae — Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
  2. It's not glue, suction or static electricity that keep geckos from falling off the ceiling — University of California, Berkeley

A direct-canvas natural-history infographic showing the male green orchid bee's brush-like scent collection, hind-tibia storage pouches, and wing-fanned courtship display, with conservative anatomy, source, sex-difference, habitat, nesting, scale, and pollination context.

  • The green orchid bee's accepted common and scientific names are green orchid bee and Euglossa dilemma, and it is an orchid bee in family Apidae and tribe Euglossini. [1]
  • Adult Euglossa dilemma are metallic green, roughly honey-bee sized, with dark transparent wings and a long tongue; males have brush-like front tarsi and enlarged hind tibiae. [1]
  • Male orchid bees collect fragrant volatile compounds from environmental sources including flowers, fungi, and decaying vegetation. [1] [2]
  • Males collect fragrance material with mop-like or brush-like structures on the front tarsi and transfer it into enlarged hind tibiae. [1]

  • Male orchid bees release the resulting perfume bouquet during wing-fanned courtship displays at perching sites. [1] [2]
  • Perfume chemistry and collection behavior can differ between closely related orchid-bee species and contribute to species-characteristic sexual signaling, but perfume should not be presented as a guaranteed mating outcome. [2]

  • Female green orchid bees build resin nest cells in enclosed cavities and provision developing young with nectar and pollen. [1]

How Nacre Turns Cracks Into Detours

A source-verified materials-science infographic showing how staggered aragonite platelets, thin organic interfaces, tortuous crack paths, bridging, friction, pull-out, and cooperative deformation work together across scales to make nacre damage-tolerant.

Research behind the infographic

  • Nacre is a hierarchical biological composite made mostly of aragonite platelets separated by a small organic matrix fraction. [1] [2]
  • The aragonite platelets form a staggered brick-and-mortar-like architecture with thin organic interfaces. [1] [2]
  • Crack deflection, crack blunting, and microcracking help create a tortuous crack path and reduce catastrophic failure. [1]
  • Organic material can bridge opening platelets and dissipate energy as cracks advance. [1]
  • Platelet pull-out and friction associated with interface nanoasperities contribute to nacre's resistance to fracture. [1] [2]
  • Cooperative deformation across co-oriented stacks of aragonite platelets adds a larger hierarchical scale to nacre toughening. [1]
  • Monolithic aragonite tends to form a more direct major crack under indentation, whereas nacre spreads damage and confines cracks near the loaded region. [1]
  • Nacre's toughness emerges from several cooperating mechanisms across scales rather than from one interface feature alone. [1] [2]

Sources

  1. Nacre toughening due to cooperative plastic deformation of stacks of co-oriented aragonite platelets — Communications Materials (Springer Nature)
  2. Multiscale mechanical studies of nacre from gastropod mollusk Trochus Nilocitus — Massachusetts Institute of Technology

Living Gears of the Issus Nymph

A museum-quality direct-canvas infographic showing how real juvenile Issus planthoppers use paired biological gear teeth on their hind legs to synchronize a jump, and how the gears vanish at the final molt.

Research behind the infographic

  • Issus coleoptratus is a jumping planthopper insect. [1] [2]
  • In Issus coleoptratus nymphs, opposing toothed strips on the two hind-leg trochantera interlock as functional gears. [1] [2]
  • The interlocking gears mechanically synchronize the propulsive hind legs during a jump. [1] [2]
  • High-speed video showed the hind legs beginning their propulsive movement within about 30 microseconds of one another. [1] [2]
  • Synchronized propulsion limits unwanted yaw that could spin the insect during takeoff. [1] [2]
  • Each juvenile gear strip is approximately 400 micrometres long and carries 10 to 12 teeth. [1] [2]
  • The two gear strips have matching tooth counts and therefore a 1:1 gearing ratio. [1] [2]
  • The teeth are asymmetric and curved because they transmit motion in the jump-launch direction rather than in both rotational directions. [1] [2]
  • Rounded tooth bases reduce stress concentration and help resist shearing. [1] [2]
  • The functional gears occur in juvenile nymphs and are lost at the final molt to adulthood. [1] [2]
  • A damaged juvenile gear may be replaced at a later molt, whereas an adult has no later molt to repair rigid cuticle. [2]
  • Adults synchronize their hind legs without the juvenile interlocking gear teeth. [1] [2]
  • The nymph is a small six-legged insect with the standard head, thorax and abdomen body regions of an insect. [1]

Sources

  1. Interacting Gears Synchronize Propulsive Leg Movements in a Jumping Insect — Science

Anna's Hummingbird — A Feather Built to Flash

A direct-canvas museum infographic tracing light from a male Anna's hummingbird gorget through feather barbules and their keratin, melanosome, and air multilayers to explain directional, angle-dependent structural color.

Research behind the infographic

  • The male Anna's hummingbird is the real species Calypte anna, and its crown and gorget include bright reddish-pink iridescent feathers. [2]
  • A feather branches from rachis to barbs to smaller barbules; the iridescent optical structures are located within the barbules. [1] [2]
  • The iridescent barbules contain stacks of melanin-bearing melanosomes embedded in and separated by keratin, with internal air spaces that create strong refractive-index contrasts. [1] [2]
  • These repeating melanosome, keratin, and air layers act as an optical multilayer whose reflections reinforce selected wavelengths and produce structural color. [1] [2]
  • The reflected color and brightness depend strongly on illumination and viewing angle, so a feather can flash brightly on-angle and become much darker when rotated off-angle. [1] [2]
  • In measured Anna's hummingbird feathers, changing the angle of incidence shifted the reflected color toward shorter wavelengths, behavior characteristic of an optical multilayer. [2]
  • The distal portion of an Anna's hummingbird gorget feather carries the strongest reddish-pink reflection, while the reflecting barbules are oriented to produce a directional, approximately specular glint. [2]
  • Hummingbirds vary in melanosome shape, stacking, air content, and feather-layer dimensions, helping produce diverse iridescent colors; not every hummingbird feather is brightly structural. [1]
  • The infographic's comparison between pigment-only absorption and structural reflection is qualitative: melanin contributes to the optical system, but nanoscale organization is essential to the iridescent effect. [1] [2]

  1. Hummingbirds' rainbow colors come from pancake-shaped structures in their feathers — Field Museum

  • The adult is flightless and its forewing-derived elytra have evolved into a solid protective shield. [1] [2]
  • Adults occur in western North America, including the U.S. Southwest and Sierra Nevada foothills, and can live beneath rocks or squeezed between tree bark and trunk. [1] [3]

  • The elytra consist of chitin layers in a protein matrix. [1]
  • The two elytral halves meet at a medial suture shaped like interlocking jigsaw-puzzle pieces. [1] [2]
  • Under compression, layered material inside the interlocking blades delaminates progressively instead of failing through a sudden catastrophic neck fracture. [1]
  • Rodlike microtrichia on the blade surfaces are interpreted as frictional pads that resist slipping. [1]
  • X-ray microtomography at the Advanced Light Source visualized the internal architecture and interlocking regions during compression. [1] [2]
  • Compression testing found that the beetle can withstand a force of about 39,000 times its body weight. [1] [2]

  • Globe skimmers require freshwater for reproduction and can develop as larvae in temporary rain pools before emerging as migratory adults. [2]
  • Pantala flavescens nymphs are aquatic predators that capture small aquatic prey with a rapidly moving modified labium. [1]
  • The extendable labium includes a postmentum, prementum, and paired labial palpi connected by articulation joints. [1]
  • During a strike, the jointed labium unfolds and protracts, the paired palpi open and then close around the prey, and the captured prey is retracted toward the mouth. [1]
  • High-speed videography documents rapid underwater protraction and retraction of the globe-skimmer nymph's labium. [1]
  • The palpi carry setae and sensilla; these are visible sensory structures, while their exact functions should not be overstated. [1]
  • Globe-skimmer nymphs have been collected from natural and artificial ponds, and mosquito larvae can be among the small aquatic prey they capture. [1]
  • The adult globe skimmer's enlarged hindwing base contributes to efficient gliding during long-distance migration. [2]

How Volcanic Plumes Make Lightning

A direct-canvas museum infographic tracing how ash fragmentation, particle collisions and clustering, charge separation, mixed-phase ice processes, and plume dynamics can combine to produce volcanic lightning and support eruption monitoring.

Research behind the infographic

  • Lightning is often observed during explosive volcanic eruptions and is commonly associated with ash-plume formation. [1]
  • Volcanic lightning can occur in the gas-thrust region near the vent, the convecting rising column, and the spreading umbrella region. [1]
  • Collisions and clustering among ash particles can generate and concentrate electrical charge in volcanic plumes. [1] [2]
  • Magma fragmentation, particle convection and buoyancy, and hydrometeor formation can all contribute to plume electrification. [1]
  • Size-dependent triboelectrification of colliding ash particles is a principal volcanic-plume charging pathway. [2]
  • Collisions among in-plume hydrometeors can add an ice-related charging pathway when water and ice form aloft. [1] [2]
  • Turbulence can preferentially concentrate particles into denser patches, increasing collision opportunities and favorable conditions for charge concentration. [2]
  • Volcanic lightning patterns and rates can provide monitoring information about otherwise obscured plume activity, although the relationship depends on plume conditions and charging mechanisms. [2]

Red Sprites — Lightning Above the Storm

A source-verified direct-canvas infographic showing how some powerful lightning events can trigger streamer-like red sprites high above thunderstorms, with their altitude, morphology, duration, and observation methods.

Research behind the infographic

  • Red sprites are short-lived red electrical discharges above thunderstorms and are connected to lightning. [1]
  • Sprites typically begin roughly 70 to 80 kilometers above thunderstorms and can develop downward over tens of kilometers. [1] [3]
  • Sprites can show long vertical tendrils, jellyfish-like forms, and grouped events. [1]
  • Sprites last only milliseconds and are difficult to see from the ground because the parent thunderstorm often blocks the view. [1]
  • A conventional sprite explanation involves brief thunderstorm electric fields after some positive cloud-to-ground lightning strokes producing streamer-like air breakdown in the middle atmosphere. [2]
  • Sprites are upper-atmosphere events distinct in location and form from the ordinary lightning occurring in or below the thunderstorm. [1] [2]
  • Sprites have been recorded from the International Space Station, aircraft, spacecraft, and distant ground viewpoints with low-light or high-speed cameras. [1] [3]
  • Airborne sprite research has used high-speed imaging and slitless spectroscopy to study spatial, temporal, and spectral structure. [3]
  • A useful scale comparison places the thunderstorm in the troposphere and the sprite high above it in the stratospheric and mesospheric region. [1] [2]
  • Not every lightning flash produces a sprite; the infographic must present the parent-lightning relationship as conditional rather than universal. [1] [2]

Sea Star Tube Feet — A Hydraulic Walking System

A source-verified museum infographic explaining how a sea star's water vascular system, ampullae, soft tube feet, and reversible adhesive secretions coordinate underwater locomotion.

Research behind the infographic

  • Sea stars are echinoderms, and their adult bodies typically have a five-part radial plan around a central axis. [1] [2]
  • A sea star's water vascular system includes a central ring canal and radial canals extending along the arms. [1]
  • Rows of tube feet project along the oral underside of each arm and connect to the radial canals. [1]
  • Individual tube feet are controlled by bulb-like ampullae and extend or retract as fluid volume changes. [1]
  • The water vascular system provides hydrostatic force used in locomotion and prey manipulation. [1]
  • The madreporite lies on the aboral surface and connects through a stone canal to the ring canal. [1]
  • Tube feet also contribute to feeding, attachment, tactile sensing, and chemical sensing. [1]
  • Sea star tube feet use specialized adhesive cells for temporary attachment to submerged surfaces. [2]
  • Attachment and release use different secretions, enabling repeated rapid adhesion and detachment during movement. [2]
  • A sea star coordinates many tube feet to move across the seabed rather than walking on a small set of jointed legs. [1] [2]

Titiwai — The Living Fishing Curtain

An insect-first direct-canvas infographic showing how the real New Zealand glow-worm larva uses blue-green bioluminescence, hanging silk lines, and hygroscopic adhesive droplets to lure, trap, and retrieve small prey.

Research behind the infographic

  • The New Zealand glow-worm is the real insect species Arachnocampa luminosa, a fungus-gnat larva rather than a worm. [1] [2]
  • Arachnocampa luminosa is endemic to New Zealand and occurs in still, dark, damp caves and forest habitats with suitable prey. [1] [2]
  • The larva lives suspended in a horizontal mucous tube attached to a ceiling or overhang. [1] [2]
  • The larva secretes silk through mouthpart-associated labial glands and lowers multiple vertical fishing lines from its tube. [1] [2]
  • The fishing lines carry regularly spaced adhesive mucous droplets that trap small insects. [1] [2]
  • The adhesive droplets are mostly water, are hygroscopic, and contain dissolved elements and peptide material; they differ from orb-spider glue droplets. [2]
  • A light organ near the larva's posterior end is associated with the Malpighian-tubule system and emits blue-green bioluminescence. [1] [2]
  • The larval glow functions as a prey lure, while the hanging adhesive lines perform the capture. [1] [2]
  • After prey sticks to a line, the larva can use its mouthparts to haul the line upward and reach the prey. [1] [2]
  • Fishing-line length varies with habitat and wind exposure, with longer lines favored in still, moist cave conditions and shorter lines in wind-prone forest habitat. [1] [2]
  • Larvae can reach about 30 millimeters before pupation, providing a supported scale cue for the whole-insect view. [1]
  • The life cycle proceeds through egg, luminous predatory larva, pupa, and winged adult fungus gnat; the larval stage is the principal feeding stage. [1] [2]
